section_summary: This section documents U.S. efforts to monitor and restrict strategic exports to Japan, including scrap iron and steel, petroleum, copper, aluminum, refinery plans, and communications supplies. It combines official regulations and intelligence reports with diplomatic correspondence about Japanese attempts to obtain tin, tungsten, oil, copper, and scrap through Latin America, China, Indochina, Manchuria, and possible transshipment routes. It also contains numerous public letters urging a broader embargo and several detailed reports on Japan’s petroleum production, refining capacity, reserves, and dependence on imports.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of conversation concerning the Olga E. Embericos
subfiles.from: Winthrop Murray Crane, Department of State
subfiles.about: Reports an Office of Naval Intelligence teletype concerning a Greek ship carrying scrap metal to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Greek ship Olga E. Embericos at Norfolk carried scrap for Japan; crew objected, but Customs found papers in order and the Navy lacked authority to stop it.

subfiles.title: Control of Iron and Steel Scrap Exports
subfiles.about: Announces expanded licensing controls on exports of iron and steel scrap.
subfiles.summary: White House release: scrap controls broadened to conserve defense supplies; No. 1 heavy melting licenses revoked, new licenses ordinarily only to the Western Hemisphere and Britain.

subfiles.title: Regulations governing exports of iron and steel scrap
subfiles.about: Defines iron and steel scrap broadly and subjects all grades to the export-control regulations.
subfiles.summary: Regulation amends the scrap definition to include all kinds and applies July 1940 regulations to scrap exports from October 16, 1940.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Colombian-Japanese trade treaty
subfiles.about: Refers to a report on a Colombian-Japanese barter arrangement involving textiles, coffee, and manganese.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Colombian-Japanese trade treaty exchanging textiles for coffee and manganese; fifty tons of manganese requested for Japanese testing.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 108: Copper Shipments to Japan
subfiles.from: George H. Adams, American Vice Consul, Antofagasta
subfiles.about: Reports recent and planned copper shipments from Antofagasta to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Adams lists copper and other mineral cargoes carried by several Japanese vessels, including cathodes supplied by the Chile Exploration Company. He notes the use of master's receipts rather than local bills of lading and identifies Mitsubishi Shoji Kaisha as handling documentation, with Osaka or Yokohama as destinations.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Tetsuo Miyakawa on embargoes
subfiles.about: Refers to information from Tetsuo Miyakawa about the effects of American and Japanese embargoes.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Miyakawa said an American embargo would seriously threaten Japan and a Japanese silk embargo would hamper parachute production.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Higashikuze on scrap and oil embargoes
subfiles.about: Refers to a warning that an embargo might drive Japan toward the Dutch East Indies.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Higashikuze said a scrap and oil embargo would force the military to seize Dutch East Indies industries.

subfiles.title: Catch sheet for file 894.24/116
subfiles.about: Provides an administrative form for charging out and returning the case file.
subfiles.summary: The sheet contains instructions for recording requests for the file or particular enclosures. No substantive diplomatic information is entered.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Aluminum routed through Brazil
subfiles.about: Refers to information about aluminum allegedly shipped to Brazil for onward shipment to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: aluminum moving from the US to Brazil and onward to Japan through New York.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Press comment on proposed embargoes
subfiles.about: Refers to Japanese press comment on proposed American embargo action.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: press telegram on a US proposal for Latin American munitions embargoes against Japan and a possible total ban on petroleum, metals and iron.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1037: Japanese press attacks on Anglo-American policy
subfiles.about: Summarizes Japanese press accusations that Britain and the United States were obstructing negotiations with the Netherlands Indies.
subfiles.summary: Japanese editorials attributed a less accommodating Netherlands Indies policy to Anglo-American pressure and denied that Japan pursued an aggressive oil policy. Other reports discussed Latin American resistance to an American munitions embargo proposal and a possible total United States ban on strategic exports to Japan.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Predicted post-election export ban
subfiles.about: Refers to a Japanese newspaper prediction of a general American export ban after the presidential election.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Grew's telegram: Japanese press suggested a broad export ban would follow the election.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Release of arms to Japan
subfiles.about: Refers to a letter commenting on United States policy in releasing arms for Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a public letter on American policy toward arms for Japan.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Japanese naval inspector in New York
subfiles.about: Refers to the assignment of a Japanese naval inspector to assist with crude-oil deliveries in New York.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Sadaki Tsuru assigned to the Japanese Navy Inspector's Office in New York, helping deliver crude oil bought in the US.

subfiles.title: Memorandum to Herbert Feis concerning a reply to Bolivia
subfiles.about: Explains that information for the American Minister in Bolivia had not yet been put into letter form.
subfiles.summary: Trueblood leaves preceding material as a memorandum for Feis to add comments before replying to the Minister in Bolivia.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Chinese tin and tungsten supplies
subfiles.about: Explains Japanese access to Chinese tin and tungsten despite not controlling the principal producing districts.
subfiles.summary: Memo: Guangdong is the main tungsten region and Yunnan the main tin area; tungsten through Japanese lines can be diverted, and Chinese tin now leaves via the Burma Road.

subfiles.title: Letter seeking information on Japanese tin and tungsten supplies
subfiles.from: Douglas Jenkins, American Minister, La Paz
subfiles.about: Asks whether Japan's access to Chinese and Indochinese minerals explains its purchasing activity in Bolivia.
subfiles.summary: Jenkins asks for an estimate of Japanese access to tin and tungsten from China and Indochina. He reports earlier Japanese barter proposals and recent rumors that Japanese interests might establish small ore-sorting plants in Bolivia, possibly to secure tungsten.

subfiles.title: Reply to Douglas Jenkins on Japanese mineral supplies
subfiles.about: Provides an assessment of Japan's access to Chinese and Indochinese tin and tungsten.
subfiles.summary: Feis explains that Japanese import secrecy prevents a precise estimate but emphasizes that the main Chinese producing regions remain outside Japanese control. He describes smuggling through Japanese lines, disrupted tin exports through Indochina, production figures, and Japanese demands that Indochinese metals and other materials be exported exclusively to Japan.

subfiles.title: Badger letter concerning refinery designs for Japan
subfiles.from: Erastus B. Badger, E. B. Badger & Sons Company
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Green, Division of Controls
subfiles.about: Requests guidance on supplying petroleum-refinery designs to a Japanese client preparing for a possible embargo.
subfiles.summary: Badger describes a longstanding contract with Tatsumi Engineering Company for simple petroleum-distillation equipment and quotes a cable requesting complete specifications so the equipment could be built in Japan or Germany. He proposes refusing any arrangement intended to circumvent a future embargo and asks whether the Department has further objections.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of telephone call with Erastus B. Badger
subfiles.from: Harold W. Moseley, Division of Controls
subfiles.about: Records advice that refinery plans for Japan probably required an export license.
subfiles.summary: Moseley told Badger that the proposed designs likely fell under the proclamation controlling equipment and plans usable in aviation-motor-fuel production. Although Badger argued that the units would make only ordinary gasoline, he accepted the recommendation to apply for a license.

subfiles.title: Duplicate memorandum of telephone call with Badger
subfiles.about: Duplicates the memorandum advising Badger to seek a license before exporting refinery designs.
subfiles.summary: This copy repeats the conclusion that even simple distillation-unit plans could be covered by the aviation-motor-fuel controls. Badger agreed to submit a formal license application describing the plans and their intended use.

subfiles.title: Second duplicate memorandum of telephone call with Badger
subfiles.about: Provides another copy of the Division of Controls memorandum concerning the Badger refinery designs.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum again records Moseley's interpretation of the September proclamation and its broad definition of aviation motor fuel. It concludes that Badger should apply for an export license before transmitting the plans to Japan.

subfiles.title: Covering letter transmitting petroleum information
subfiles.about: Apparently transmits a copy of Walden's petroleum-shipment letter to E. J. Sadler.
subfiles.summary: Cover letter, mostly illegible, by which Walden sent Hornbeck a copy of his November 4 letter to E. J. Sadler.

subfiles.title: Letter on tanker shortages and gasoline shipments to Japan
subfiles.about: Reports tanker movements and shipments of petroleum and sub-87-octane gasoline to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Walden supplies figures dividing California petroleum liftings between Japanese and non-Japanese tankers and estimates that tanker scarcity had reduced monthly shipments. He also reports large drum and bulk orders for gasoline just below the embargoed octane level, noting that shipment delays would discourage major new purchases.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Walden petroleum report
subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt of Walden's letter and its enclosure.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck thanks Walden for the November 4 letter and the copy of his letter to Sadler.

subfiles.title: Routing memorandum on the Deming letter
subfiles.about: Directs Hamilton to answer an incoming public letter.
subfiles.summary: The Under Secretary asks Hamilton to prepare the response. The instruction relates to the following letter from W. C. Deming.

subfiles.title: W. C. Deming letter urging an embargo on Japan
subfiles.about: Urges an embargo on war supplies and imports involving Japan and greater assistance to China.
subfiles.summary: Deming urges embargoing war supplies to Japan, restricting Japanese imports and helping China.

subfiles.title: Reply to W. C. Deming
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Deming's views on the Far Eastern situation.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton, for Welles, thanks Deming and says his views are noted.

subfiles.title: Routing memorandum on the Appleton letter
subfiles.about: Directs Hamilton to answer William Sumner Appleton's letter.
subfiles.summary: Under Secretary asks Hamilton to prepare a reply to Appleton's letter.

subfiles.title: Appleton letter opposing aid to Japan
subfiles.about: Calls for ending material assistance to Japan and giving war supplies to China and Great Britain.
subfiles.summary: Appleton urges preventing American materials aiding Japan and favors gifts of war matériel to China and Britain even at greater risk of involvement.

subfiles.title: Reply to William Sumner Appleton
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Appleton's views on the Far Eastern situation.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton, for Welles, assures Appleton his views are noted and appreciated.

subfiles.title: Committee letter alleging scrap transshipment to Japan
subfiles.from: Roger S. Greene, Committee to Defend America by Aiding the Allies
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Green, Division of Controls
subfiles.about: Forwards a Seattle report alleging plans to route scrap to Japan through the Philippines or Mexico.
subfiles.summary: Greene quotes Judge Griffiths that scrap may be exported to the Philippines or Mexico for reshipment to Japan and asks Controls to investigate.

subfiles.title: Reply concerning alleged scrap transshipment
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, Division of Controls
subfiles.to: Roger S. Greene, Committee to Defend America by Aiding the Allies
subfiles.about: Explains the scrap-export regulations and requests further details about the alleged scheme.
subfiles.summary: Green encloses the September White House release and regulations limiting scrap exports to Great Britain and Western Hemisphere destinations. He states that the rules prohibit direct or indirect shipment elsewhere and asks Judge Griffiths to provide any additional details for investigation.

subfiles.title: Routing memorandum on the Welling letter
subfiles.about: Directs Hamilton to answer Richard Welling's letter.
subfiles.summary: The Under Secretary asks Hamilton to prepare a response. The instruction relates to Welling's appeal for broader embargoes against Japan.

subfiles.title: Richard Welling letter advocating broader embargoes
subfiles.about: Urges immediate extension of embargoes to copper, gasoline, motor vehicles, and other war-related supplies.
subfiles.summary: Welling is surprised key materials still reach Japan, cites a Gallup poll, and asks further action without delay.

subfiles.title: Reply to Richard Welling
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Welling's views about policy in the Far East.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton, for Welles, says Welling's letter is noted and appreciated.

subfiles.title: Alexander Henry Carver letter requesting a complete embargo
subfiles.about: Argues that all American materials usable for Japanese warfare should be embargoed.
subfiles.summary: Carver says aiding Britain while supplying Japan is inconsistent, harming China, strengthening the Axis and endangering the US.

subfiles.title: Reply to Alexander Henry Carver
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Carver's letter about the Far Eastern situation.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton replies at the request of Under Secretary Welles. He thanks Carver for bringing his views to the Department's attention.

subfiles.title: John W. Morgan letter on aid to China and restrictions on Japan
subfiles.about: Advocates increased aid to China and tighter trade restrictions on Japan following the election.
subfiles.summary: Morgan argues stronger non-provocative Far Eastern pressure would ease British demands and protect Suez against an Axis eastern Mediterranean victory.

subfiles.title: Reply to John W. Morgan
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Morgan's views on Far Eastern policy.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton replies on behalf of Under Secretary Welles. He assures Morgan that his views have been carefully noted and appreciated.

subfiles.title: Bessie C. Stern letter supporting stronger restrictions on Japan
subfiles.about: Urges embargoes on strategic exports to Japan and greater aid to China.
subfiles.summary: Stern welcomes Roosevelt's reelection as an endorsement of existing foreign policy but asks why scrap, copper, oil, gasoline, vehicles, and machinery still reach Japan. She cites public support for embargoes and argues that stronger action would improve American security while resisting Japanese aggression.

subfiles.title: Reply to Bessie C. Stern
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Stern's views on Far Eastern policy.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton, for Welles, thanks Bessie Stern for her interest and views.

subfiles.title: Japanese Embassy memorandum on the Universal Oil Products contract
subfiles.about: Requests a license permitting export of petroleum processes not directly related to high-quality aviation gasoline.
subfiles.summary: Japanese Embassy thanks the Department for permitting the 1928 contract performance and proposes a limited export license for the blocked 1938 contract in exchange for withdrawing the damage suit, reserving aviation-gasoline rights.

subfiles.title: Duplicate Japanese Embassy memorandum on petroleum processes
subfiles.about: Duplicates the proposal for a restricted license covering non-aviation-gasoline processes.
subfiles.summary: This copy repeats the history of the companies' contracts, the moral embargo, and the resulting damage suit. It proposes an amicable settlement allowing export of processes unrelated to high-quality aviation gasoline while shelving the disputed aviation-fuel rights.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Japanese Embassy memoranda
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the Embassy's proposals concerning contracts between Universal Oil Products and Japan Gasoline Company.
subfiles.summary: Department acknowledges the Embassy's memoranda and will duly consider the proposals on the 1938 contract.

subfiles.title: Justice Department transmittal of petroleum reports
subfiles.from: J. Edgar Hoover, Department of Justice
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle Jr., Department of State
subfiles.about: Transmits intelligence material concerning Japan's petroleum situation.
subfiles.summary: Degraded Justice Department cover letter to Berle transmitting numbered petroleum reports.

subfiles.title: Report No. 211: Recent Developments in Japan's Petroleum Situation
subfiles.about: Assesses Japanese refinery expansion, tanker shortages, and synthetic-fuel efforts in anticipation of an American embargo.
subfiles.summary: The report states that Japan expected imminent restrictions on fuel and lubricating oils but lacked sufficient refinery equipment and tankers to meet demand. It reviews government organization of tanker use, oil-field development, and low-temperature coal-distillation enterprises, concluding that synthetic plants were small and largely emergency standbys.

subfiles.title: Report No. 212: Petroleum in Manchukuo
subfiles.about: Evaluates claimed oil discoveries and established shale-oil and refining operations in Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: The report treats claims of a major discovery near Fuxin skeptically, noting earlier judgments that Manchuria lacked commercially useful conventional reserves. It provides production and capacity information for the Fushun shale works, a coal-liquefaction plant, and refineries at Fushun and Dalian.

subfiles.title: Report No. 213: Japanese Oil Production, Imports, and Refineries
subfiles.about: Surveys Japan's petroleum output, reserves, consumption, imports, rationing, and refinery capacity.
subfiles.summary: Report 213: Japanese domestic oil covers a small fraction of needs; underground reserves for the services; dependence on American crude and fuel oil; gasoline rationing; major refineries and capacities.

subfiles.title: Canadian letter on proposed Japanese purchases of Peruvian crude
subfiles.from: Merchant Mahoney, Canadian chargé d'affaires ad interim
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese inquiries about purchasing five monthly cargoes of Peruvian crude oil.
subfiles.summary: Mahoney reports Mitsui approached International Petroleum through Standard Vacuum about five 100,000-barrel cargoes and Asano Bussan planned to send a representative to Peru.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Canadian petroleum information
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the report of Japanese approaches for Peruvian crude oil.
subfiles.summary: Hickerson states that he read Mahoney's letter with interest. He thanks the Canadian chargé for forwarding the information.

subfiles.title: Instruction forwarding Canadian report to Lima
subfiles.to: American chargé d'affaires ad interim, Lima
subfiles.about: Forwards the Canadian chargé's report on Japanese negotiations for Peruvian petroleum.
subfiles.summary: Department sends Lima a confidential copy of Mahoney's November 27 letter to support local inquiry into Japanese purchasing.

subfiles.title: Follow-up reply on investigation of Japanese oil interests in Peru
subfiles.about: Reports the Lima Embassy's findings on alleged Japanese efforts to acquire Peruvian petroleum.
subfiles.summary: The International Petroleum Company's general manager said discussions had occurred before he left New York but that he had heard nothing further after returning to Peru. Neither he nor the Peruvian foreign and commerce ministries knew of the reported arrival of an Asano Bussan representative to survey oil fields.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1341: Perforated paper used by Japanese communications services
subfiles.about: Suggests controlling exports of specialized paper needed by Japanese automatic telegraph and radio systems.
subfiles.summary: Telegram 1341: an American expert says Japanese automatic communications depend on perforated paper made only in Philadelphia, London and Berlin; suggests embargoing it.

subfiles.title: Inter-Professional Association letter on oil-company sales to Japan
subfiles.about: Questions whether American-controlled oil sales from the Dutch East Indies undermine United States policy toward Japan.
subfiles.summary: Inter-Professional Association asks whether American and Shell oil sales to Japan, per a reported Dutch East Indies agreement, conflict with Department restrictions.

subfiles.title: Copy of confidential copper-booking list
subfiles.about: Lists copper cathode cargoes booked for Japanese vessels through January 1941.
subfiles.summary: Confidential copper-booking list: five vessels, parcel weights, loading dates and destinations, mostly for Mitsubishi Shoji Kaisha to Yokohama or Osaka.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 113: Additional Copper Shipments to Japan
subfiles.from: George H. Adams, American Vice Consul, Antofagasta
subfiles.about: Reports additional bookings of Chilean copper for shipment to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Despatch 113: Adams reports further semi-refined copper shipments by Chile Exploration Company and forwards the booking list.

subfiles.title: Confidential list of copper shipments booked for Japan
subfiles.from: Confidential source, American Consulate at Antofagasta
subfiles.about: Details planned copper cargoes and emphasizes protection of the confidential source.
subfiles.summary: The enclosure lists the Venice Maru, Hie Maru, Noruto Maru, Norway Maru, and Taroaka Maru, with parcel sizes and expected loading dates. It identifies Yokohama and Osaka as destinations and warns that the source must not be disclosed under any circumstances.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1193: Japanese Interest in Purchasing Scrap Iron
subfiles.about: Reports a Japanese banking inquiry seeking Colombian firms able to supply scrap iron.
subfiles.summary: Despatch 1193: Yokohama Specie Bank's New York office asked Banco Alemán Antioqueño for names of creditworthy Colombian scrap-iron sellers.

subfiles.title: Memorandum forwarding report on Japanese scrap purchases
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, Division of Controls
subfiles.about: Forwards the Bogotá Embassy's report about Japanese interest in Colombian scrap iron.
subfiles.summary: Yost sends the Administrator the Embassy's November 28 despatch on Japanese efforts to identify Colombian scrap suppliers.
